Senior management has business information that they do not share with the technical team, which leads to the design or implementation of incorrect solutions. Many times they do not share it not only with bad intentions, but they also assume that everyone (magically) knows what they know.    . There are teams and people who are open to feedback and others who are not. For example, many times the Sales area is not open to feedback from the Technical Team when it comes to improving the pre-sale Requirements Gathering. This causes bad scoping dynamics to be perpetuated.    . I love remote work, but communication often becomes more complex, slower, and requires much more effort.    . Different backgrounds or knowledge lead us to express the same concepts using different words. This sometimes creates misalignment between teams. For example: Project Managers talk about the different milestones of a project using words that differ from those used by the Technical team. This leads to problems regarding task delivery, commitment to meeting certain deadlines, misunderstood project expectations, etc. This is just one example that can be extended to collaborative work between different teams. I believe that referring to  requirements  causes confusion for customers/users & teams as we need to distinguish between understanding and documenting the business or user problem we are solving, and the solution approach that will be captured in user stories and dictates the way the product operates. I prefer to use  problem  and  solution  to distinguish between discovery of the problem space (done by Product Manager/Product Owners/Product Designers) and agreeing a solution approach (done with Product team and lead engineers). We should expect and anticipate that problems and solutions will change and evolve.
